questions.question: Classify: 'Kathmandu's air quality exceeds WHO limits' and 'Kathmandu is the most beautiful city in the world'.
questions.solution: First: FACT — measurable, verifiable against data. Second: OPINION — a value judgement ('most beautiful') that cannot be verified. The test: can it be checked against evidence independently of who says it? Mixing the two is how persuasion disguises itself as information.

questions.question: 'My neighbour's dog bit me; all dogs are dangerous.' What is the fallacy and why does it fail?
questions.solution: Hasty generalisation — drawing a universal conclusion from one (or too few) instances. One dog cannot represent all dogs; the sample is far too small and possibly biased (that particular dog's history). Valid generalisation needs a large, representative sample.

questions.question: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer. Does ice-cream cause drowning? Explain the correct reasoning.
questions.solution: No — both rise because of a THIRD factor: hot weather sends more people swimming AND raises ice-cream sales. Correlation (moving together) does not establish cause; a confounding variable may drive both. Establishing cause requires a mechanism and controlled comparison, not just coincidence in the data.

questions.question: 'You can't trust his argument on climate — he drives a big car.' Name the fallacy and explain why the argument's merit is untouched.
questions.solution: Ad hominem — attacking the PERSON instead of the argument. An argument stands or falls on its EVIDENCE and logic, not on the speaker's lifestyle; hypocrisy may be relevant to character but does not refute a claim. The correct response is to examine the evidence, not the messenger.

questions.question: Two articles claim a herb cures colds: one cites a controlled trial of 500 patients; the other cites 'thousands of satisfied users'. Which is stronger evidence and why?
questions.solution: The controlled trial — it isolates the herb's effect from placebo and natural recovery, uses a defined sample and reports methods others can check. 'Satisfied users' is anecdote: no control group, self-selected, unverifiable. Strength of evidence = design quality (control, sample, transparency), not volume of testimony.

questions.question: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together. Why is concluding 'ice cream causes drowning' an error of reasoning?
questions.solution: Both are driven by a shared third factor — hot weather brings more swimming and more ice-cream buying. A correlation establishes co-variation, not a mechanism; a confounder can produce it with no causal link. Causal claims need either controlled comparison or a plausible mechanism excluding confounders. Two things moving together says nothing about which moves which.

questions.question: Why does one vivid personal story so often feel more persuasive than a large statistical study, even though the study is stronger evidence?
questions.solution: Anecdotes are concrete, emotionally available and easy to recall, so they trigger the availability heuristic and feel representative; statistics are abstract and require interpretation. But a single case cannot establish a rate or exclude chance, while aggregated data can. The feeling of persuasiveness is a property of the presentation, not of the evidence's strength — this is exactly the bias critical thinking must correct for.

questions.concept: Why a straw man is a fallacy
questions.question: Why does refuting a distorted version of an opponent's argument fail to refute the argument itself?
questions.solution: A refutation is only valid against the claim it actually addresses. Weakening or exaggerating the opponent's position produces a claim they never made, so defeating it leaves the real argument untouched while creating the impression of victory. The error is one of relevance: the conclusion does not follow from the premise because the premise targets a different claim.
